Title: GRIN2B encephalopathy: novel findings on phenotype, variant clustering, functional consequences and treatment aspects.
Authors: Konrad Platzer; Hongjie Yuan; Hannah Schütz; Alexander Winschel; Wenjuan Chen; Chun Hu; Hirofumi Kusumoto; Henrike O Heyne; Katherine L Helbig; Sha Tang; Marcia C Willing; Brad T Tinkle; Darius J Adams; Christel Depienne; Boris Keren; Cyril Mignot; Eirik Frengen; Petter Strømme; Saskia Biskup; Dennis Döcker; Tim M Strom; Heather C Mefford; Candace T Myers; Alison M Muir; Amy LaCroix; Lynette Sadleir; Ingrid E Scheffer; Eva Brilstra; Mieke M van Haelst; Jasper J van der Smagt; Levinus A Bok; Rikke S Møller; Uffe B Jensen; John J Millichap; Anne T Berg; Ethan M Goldberg; Isabelle De Bie; Stephanie Fox; Philippe Major; Julie R Jones; Elaine H Zackai; Rami Abou Jamra; Arndt Rolfs; Richard J Leventer; John A Lawson; Tony Roscioli; Floor E Jansen; Emmanuelle Ranza; Christian M Korff; Anna-Elina Lehesjoki; Carolina Courage; Tarja Linnankivi; Douglas R Smith; Christine Stanley; Mark Mintz; Dianalee McKnight; Amy Decker; Wen-Hann Tan; Mark A Tarnopolsky; Lauren I Brady; Markus Wolff; Lutz Dondit; Helio F Pedro; Sarah E Parisotto; Kelly L Jones; Anup D Patel; David N Franz; Rena Vanzo; Elysa Marco; Judith D Ranells; Nataliya Di Donato; William B Dobyns; Bodo Laube; Stephen F Traynelis; Johannes R Lemke
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We aimed for a comprehensive delineation of genetic, functional and phenotypic aspects of GRIN2B encephalopathy and explored potential prospects of personalised medicine.
METHODS: Data of 48 individuals with de novo GRIN2B variants were collected from several diagnostic and research cohorts, as well as from 43 patients from the literature. Functional consequences and response to memantine treatment were investigated in vitro and eventually translated into patient care.
RESULTS: Overall, de novo variants in 86 patients were classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic. Patients presented with neurodevelopmental disorders and a spectrum of hypotonia, movement disorder, cortical visual impairment, cerebral volume loss and epilepsy. Six patients presented with a consistent malformation of cortical development (MCD) intermediate between tubulinopathies and polymicrogyria. Missense variants cluster in transmembrane segments and ligand-binding sites. Functional consequences of variants were diverse, revealing various potential gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms and a retained sensitivity to the use-dependent blocker memantine. However, an objectifiable beneficial treatment response in the respective patients still remains to be demonstrated.
CONCLUSIONS: In addition to previously known features of intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism, we found evidence that GRIN2B encephalopathy is also frequently associated with movement disorder, cortical visual impairment and MCD revealing novel phenotypic consequences of channelopathies.

summary.text: Researchers studied GRIN2B encephalopathy, a brain condition linked to new gene changes, looking at its genetic, laboratory and patient features and at possible personalised treatment.

verification.reason: Whole-summary audit: Every factual clause matches the source abstract and the cited claims. The cohort sizes (48 new patients plus 43 from earlier reports) are accurate. The listed features are accurate: low muscle tone, loss of brain volume, epilepsy, movement problems and brain-caused vision problems. The six patients with a consistent brain-formation difference are accurate. Intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism are correctly described as already known. The caveat that a clear benefit of memantine in patients has not been shown is kept. Plain-language paraphrases such as 'vision problems caused by the brain' and 'difference in how the outer brain layer had formed' add no new scientific claims, and the wording is accessible. Omitted secondary details are the variant clustering, the 86-patient pathogenicity classification, and the lab result that variant effects were diverse while memantine sensitivity was retained. These do not undermine the central design, the phenotype findings or the treatment caveat.

candidate.statement: De novo variants in 86 patients were classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic.
candidate.quote: RESULTS: Overall, de novo variants in 86 patients were classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic. Patients presented with neurodevelopmental disorders and a spectrum of hypotonia, movement disorder, cortical visual impairment, cerebral volume loss and epilepsy. Six patients presented with a consistent malformation of cortical development (MCD) intermediate between tubulinopathies and polymicrogyria. Missense variants cluster in transmembrane segments and ligand-binding sites. Functional consequences of variants were diverse, revealing various potential gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms and a retained sensitivity to the use-dependent blocker memantine. However, an objectifiable beneficial treatment response in the respective patients still remains to be demonstrated.

E5.quote: RESULTS: Overall, de novo variants in 86 patients were classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic. Patients presented with neurodevelopmental disorders and a spectrum of hypotonia, movement disorder, cortical visual impairment, cerebral volume loss and epilepsy. Six patients presented with a consistent malformation of cortical development (MCD) intermediate between tubulinopathies and polymicrogyria. Missense variants cluster in transmembrane segments and ligand-binding sites. Functional consequences of variants were diverse, revealing various potential gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms and a retained sensitivity to the use-dependent blocker memantine. However, an objectifiable beneficial treatment response in the respective patients still remains to be demonstrated.

sentences.text: The study aimed to describe the genetic, functional and clinical features of GRIN2B encephalopathy and to explore prospects for personalised medicine.
The researchers collected data on 48 individuals with new (de novo) GRIN2B gene variants from diagnostic and research cohorts, plus 43 patients from published reports.
The researchers also tested the functional effects of the variants and the response to memantine in laboratory (in vitro) experiments, and then applied this to patient care.
The patients showed a range of features, including low muscle tone (hypotonia), cerebral volume loss and epilepsy.
Six patients had a consistent malformation of cortical development that was intermediate between tubulinopathies and polymicrogyria.

The authors concluded that GRIN2B encephalopathy is frequently linked to cortical visual impairment and malformation of cortical development, in addition to the previously known features of autism and epilepsy.
The benefit of memantine for patients has not been shown: an objectifiable beneficial treatment response in patients still remains to be demonstrated.

rejected.reason: Every clause is entailed by the cited claims. The sentences are complete, readable and in a coherent order. The memantine caveat (no beneficial treatment response yet shown in patients) is preserved. The summary omits central results from the source. It says the researchers tested functional effects of variants but never reports what they found: diverse gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms, and retained in vitro sensitivity to memantine. It also omits that missense variants cluster in transmembrane segments and ligand-binding sites, and that 86 patients in total had variants classed as pathogenic or likely pathogenic. The supplied claims do not cover these results either. The memantine sentence therefore lacks the in vitro finding it contrasts with. Revision needs claims for the functional and variant-clustering results, and the summary should state them.

The six patients with a consistent brain-formation difference are accurate. Intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism are correctly described as already known. The caveat that a clear benefit of memantine in patients has not been shown is kept. Plain-language paraphrases such as 'vision problems caused by the brain' and 'difference in how the outer brain layer had formed' add no new scientific claims, and the wording is accessible. Omitted secondary details are the variant clustering, the 86-patient pathogenicity classification, and the lab result that variant effects were diverse while memantine sensitivity was retained. These do not undermine the central design, the phenotype findings or the treatment caveat.
